title: General Zoology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 100L general zoology syllabus: scope of zoology, taxonomy and classification, animal cell structure, tissue levels of organisation, symmetry and body plans, survey of the major invertebrate and vertebrate phyla, and basic physiology/ecology concepts every first-year zoology student must know.

questions.question: Zoology is best defined as the branch of biology concerned with the study of:
questions.explanation: Zoology (from Greek zoon, animal) is the scientific study of animals, including their structure, function, classification, behaviour, and distribution.

questions.question: The branch of zoology that deals with the classification of animals into groups is called:
questions.explanation: Taxonomy is the science of naming, describing, and classifying organisms into a hierarchical system of categories.

questions.question: The system of giving every organism a two-part scientific name (genus and species) is known as:
questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature, introduced by Carl Linnaeus, gives each species a unique two-part Latinised name consisting of genus and specific epithet.

questions.question: Arrange the following taxonomic categories from the broadest to the most specific: Class, Family, Genus, Kingdom, Order, Phylum, Species.
options: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Order, Family, Species, Genus
Phylum, Kingdom, Class, Family, Order, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Order, Class, Family, Genus, Species
questions.correct_answer: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
questions.explanation: The standard Linnaean hierarchy proceeds from the broadest category (Kingdom) down to the most specific (Species): Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.

questions.question: In the taxonomic hierarchy, which category is generally regarded as the basic unit of classification?
questions.explanation: The species is the fundamental, basic taxonomic unit, defined as a group of organisms capable of interbreeding and producing fertile offspring.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the generally accepted characteristics of living organisms?
questions.explanation: Crystallisation is a physical process of non-living matter; it is not a life characteristic. Living things show nutrition, respiration, excretion, growth, reproduction, movement, and irritability.

questions.question: A major structural feature that distinguishes a typical animal cell from a typical plant cell is that the animal cell:
options: Lacks a cell wall and chloroplasts
questions.correct_answer: Lacks a cell wall and chloroplasts
questions.explanation: Animal cells have only a plasma membrane (no rigid cell wall) and do not contain chloroplasts, unlike plant cells.

questions.question: The organelle responsible for generating most of the cell's ATP through aerobic respiration is the:
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic cellular respiration and produce most of the ATP that powers cellular activities.

questions.question: Ribosomes, whether free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, are primarily responsible for:
questions.explanation: Ribosomes translate messenger RNA into polypeptide chains, making them the cell's site of protein synthesis.

questions.question: The plasma membrane of an animal cell is best described as:
options: Selectively permeable, controlling movement of substances in and out of the cell
Freely permeable to all substances without regulation
Rigid and made mainly of cellulose
questions.correct_answer: Selectively permeable, controlling movement of substances in and out of the cell
questions.explanation: The plasma membrane's phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins allows selective, regulated passage of ions and molecules.

questions.question: The correct order of increasing complexity in the levels of biological organisation in a multicellular animal is:
options: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
Tissue, cell, organ, organism, organ system
Organ, tissue, cell, organism, organ system
Cell, organ, tissue, organism, organ system
questions.correct_answer: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
questions.explanation: Cells group into tissues, tissues into organs, organs into organ systems, and organ systems together make up the organism.

questions.question: Which type of animal tissue is specialised for rapid transmission of electrical impulses?
questions.explanation: Nervous tissue is made up of neurons specialised to generate and conduct electrical impulses for communication and coordination.

questions.question: Epithelial tissue in animals primarily functions to:
options: Cover body surfaces and line cavities and organs
questions.correct_answer: Cover body surfaces and line cavities and organs
questions.explanation: Epithelial tissue forms protective, absorptive, or secretory sheets covering external surfaces and lining internal cavities, ducts, and organs.

questions.question: An animal that can be divided into similar halves by any plane passing through its central axis is said to exhibit:
questions.explanation: Radially symmetrical animals, such as cnidarians and adult echinoderms, can be cut into similar halves by any plane through the central axis.

questions.question: Bilateral symmetry, in which the body can be divided into mirror-image left and right halves by only one plane, is characteristic of:
options: Most active, motile animals such as arthropods and vertebrates
questions.correct_answer: Most active, motile animals such as arthropods and vertebrates
questions.explanation: Bilateral symmetry, associated with cephalisation and directional movement, is found in most actively moving animals including arthropods, molluscs, and chordates.

questions.question: Sponges (phylum Porifera) are best described in terms of body symmetry as:
questions.explanation: Most sponges lack any definite plane of symmetry and are classed as asymmetrical animals.

questions.question: An animal whose body develops from only two embryonic germ layers (ectoderm and endoderm) is described as:
questions.explanation: Diploblastic animals, such as cnidarians, develop from two germ layers with a non-cellular mesoglea between them, unlike triploblastic animals which have a true mesoderm.

questions.question: An animal with a true, mesoderm-lined body cavity that completely surrounds the gut is described as:
questions.explanation: Eucoelomates (e.g. annelids, molluscs, arthropods, chordates) possess a true coelom fully lined by mesoderm on all sides.

questions.question: Roundworms such as Ascaris possess a body cavity that is only partly lined by mesoderm. This is termed a:
questions.explanation: Nematodes have a pseudocoelom, a body cavity derived from the embryonic blastocoel that is not fully lined by mesoderm.

questions.question: Protozoa (e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium) are unicellular organisms placed in the animal-like protists because they:
options: Are eukaryotic, heterotrophic, and lack a cell wall
Possess a rigid cellulose cell wall
questions.correct_answer: Are eukaryotic, heterotrophic, and lack a cell wall
questions.explanation: Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes that feed heterotrophically and, unlike plant cells, have no rigid cell wall.

questions.question: Amoeba moves and captures food using temporary cytoplasmic extensions called:
questions.explanation: Amoeba extends temporary finger-like or lobed projections of cytoplasm called pseudopodia for locomotion and phagocytosis of food.

questions.question: Paramecium is characterised by locomotory organelles called:
questions.explanation: Paramecium is covered in numerous short, hair-like cilia that beat rhythmically to propel the organism through water.

questions.question: Plasmodium, the protozoan parasite that causes malaria in humans, is transmitted by the bite of an infected:
questions.explanation: Only the female Anopheles mosquito takes blood meals (needed for egg production) and thereby transmits Plasmodium sporozoites to humans.

questions.question: Sponges (phylum Porifera) feed by filtering food particles from water drawn through their bodies by the beating of flagella on specialised cells called:
questions.explanation: Choanocytes, or collar cells, line the internal canals of sponges; their flagella create water currents and their collars trap food particles for phagocytosis.

questions.question: The skeletal support in many sponges is provided by small, hard structures called:
questions.explanation: Spicules, made of calcium carbonate, silica, or protein (spongin fibres), form the internal skeleton that supports the sponge body.

questions.question: Members of the phylum Cnidaria (e.g. Hydra, jellyfish, corals) possess specialised stinging cells called:
questions.explanation: Cnidocytes house nematocysts, coiled thread-like structures that discharge to sting, capture prey, and defend the animal.

questions.question: Hydra, a common freshwater cnidarian, exists mainly in which body form?
questions.explanation: Hydra is a sessile or slow-moving polyp attached at its base, unlike jellyfish which exist mainly as the free-swimming medusa form.

questions.question: Flatworms of the phylum Platyhelminthes have which type of body cavity arrangement?
options: Acoelomate (no body cavity between gut and body wall)
questions.correct_answer: Acoelomate (no body cavity between gut and body wall)
questions.explanation: Platyhelminths are triploblastic but acoelomate; the space between their gut and body wall is filled with solid mesodermal tissue (parenchyma).

questions.question: The tapeworm Taenia solium, a parasitic flatworm found in humans, characteristically lacks a:
questions.explanation: Taenia has no mouth or gut; it absorbs already-digested nutrients directly across its body wall (tegument) from the host's intestine.

questions.question: The roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, a common human intestinal parasite, belongs to which phylum?
questions.explanation: Ascaris is a large intestinal roundworm classified in phylum Nematoda, characterised by an unsegmented, elongated, cylindrical body.

questions.question: The division of the body into a linear series of similar repeating units, as seen in earthworms, is called:
questions.explanation: Metamerism is the repetition of similar body segments along the antero-posterior axis, a defining feature of annelids.

questions.question: The earthworm (e.g. Lumbricus) is placed in phylum Annelida mainly because of its:
options: Segmented body with a true coelom
questions.correct_answer: Segmented body with a true coelom
questions.explanation: Annelids are characterised by metameric (segmented) bodies with a spacious, fluid-filled true coelom that acts as a hydrostatic skeleton.

questions.question: Which of the following is a defining feature of most molluscs (phylum Mollusca)?
options: A soft body usually protected by a shell secreted by the mantle
Jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton
A body divided into repeating metameric segments
questions.correct_answer: A soft body usually protected by a shell secreted by the mantle
questions.explanation: Molluscs typically have a soft, unsegmented body with a muscular foot, a visceral mass, and a mantle that often secretes a calcareous shell.

questions.question: Snails belong to which class of Mollusca?
questions.explanation: Gastropods, including snails and slugs, are characterised by a single (often coiled) shell or its absence, and a broad, flat muscular foot.

questions.question: Octopuses and squids belong to the molluscan class:
questions.explanation: Cephalopods have a foot modified into arms/tentacles around the head, a highly developed nervous system, and (in most living forms) a reduced or absent shell.

questions.question: Phylum Arthropoda, the largest animal phylum, is characterised by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: An internal skeleton made of bone
questions.correct_answer: An internal skeleton made of bone
questions.explanation: Arthropods have an external skeleton (exoskeleton) made of chitin, not an internal bony skeleton; that feature belongs to vertebrates.

questions.question: Because their exoskeleton cannot expand, arthropods must periodically shed it to grow, a process called:
questions.explanation: Ecdysis, or moulting, is the periodic shedding of the rigid exoskeleton that allows an arthropod's body to increase in size before a new, larger cuticle hardens.

questions.question: Insects (class Insecta) are distinguished from other arthropod classes by having:
options: Three pairs of walking legs and a body divided into head, thorax, and abdomen
Four pairs of walking legs and two body regions
Numerous pairs of legs, one or two per body segment
No antennae and a single body region
questions.correct_answer: Three pairs of walking legs and a body divided into head, thorax, and abdomen
questions.explanation: Insects have a tagmatised body of head, thorax, and abdomen, with exactly three pairs of legs attached to the thorax, distinguishing them from arachnids and crustaceans.

questions.question: Spiders and scorpions, which have four pairs of walking legs and no antennae, belong to the arthropod class:
questions.explanation: Arachnids characteristically have a cephalothorax and abdomen, four pairs of legs, and lack antennae, distinguishing them from insects.

questions.question: The unique internal water-based hydraulic system used by echinoderms (e.g. starfish) for locomotion and feeding is called the:
questions.explanation: The water vascular system, with its tube feet operated by hydraulic pressure, is a defining feature unique to echinoderms.

questions.question: Adult echinoderms such as starfish and sea urchins typically show which type of body symmetry?
questions.explanation: Adult echinoderms usually display pentaradial symmetry (five-part radial arrangement), although their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.

questions.question: Which of the following is a defining diagnostic feature shared by all chordates at some stage of their life?
options: A notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, and post-anal tail
A jointed exoskeleton and compound eyes
A water vascular system with tube feet
questions.correct_answer: A notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, and post-anal tail
questions.explanation: These four features define phylum Chordata; they may be present only in the embryo or larva of some species and lost or modified in the adult.

questions.question: In most adult vertebrates, the embryonic notochord is largely replaced by the:
questions.explanation: During vertebrate development, the cartilaginous or bony vertebral column forms around and largely replaces the embryonic notochord.

questions.question: An organism that manufactures its own food from inorganic substances using light energy is said to be:
questions.explanation: Autotrophs, mainly green plants and some protists, synthesise their own organic food, typically via photosynthesis; animals, by contrast, are heterotrophic.

questions.question: An animal that feeds exclusively on plant material is classified nutritionally as a(n):
questions.explanation: Herbivores obtain their nutrition solely from plant material, in contrast to carnivores (which eat other animals) and omnivores (which eat both).

questions.question: Gaseous exchange across the moist body surface, without specialised respiratory organs, is termed:
questions.explanation: Cutaneous (skin) respiration occurs when gases diffuse directly across a thin, moist body surface, as seen in earthworms and, partly, amphibians.

questions.question: Fish extract dissolved oxygen from water using respiratory organs called:
questions.explanation: Gills are thin, highly vascularised structures that allow efficient diffusion of oxygen from water into the blood and carbon dioxide out.

questions.question: Insects respire using a network of air-conducting tubes that open to the exterior through openings called:
questions.explanation: Insects have a tracheal system: air enters through spiracles on the body surface and is carried directly to tissues through branching tracheal tubes.

questions.question: In freshwater protozoans such as Amoeba, excess water entering the cell by osmosis is expelled by the:
questions.explanation: The contractile vacuole periodically collects and expels excess water that enters the cell by osmosis, helping to regulate internal water balance (osmoregulation).

questions.question: The excretory structures found in flatworms, which help regulate water balance, are called:
questions.explanation: Flame cells are ciliated excretory cells forming a protonephridial system in flatworms, drawing fluid through tubules for expulsion.

questions.question: The excretory organs typical of the earthworm, arranged one pair per segment, are called:
questions.explanation: Earthworms possess paired nephridia in most body segments, which filter coelomic fluid and expel nitrogenous waste to the exterior.

questions.question: The excretory structures of most insects, which extract nitrogenous waste from the haemolymph and empty into the gut, are the:
questions.explanation: Malpighian tubules are blind-ending tubules that absorb waste from the haemolymph and discharge it into the hindgut for elimination with faeces, conserving water.

questions.question: A method of asexual reproduction in which an organism splits into two roughly equal daughter individuals, seen in Amoeba, is:
questions.explanation: Binary fission is a form of asexual reproduction in which a parent cell divides into two approximately equal daughter cells, typical of many protozoans.

questions.question: In Hydra, a small outgrowth develops on the parent's body, eventually detaching as a new individual. This asexual process is called:
questions.explanation: Budding involves an outgrowth (bud) forming on the parent that develops into a complete new organism before detaching, common in Hydra under favourable conditions.

questions.question: An organism, such as the earthworm, that possesses both male and female reproductive organs in the same individual is described as:
questions.explanation: Earthworms are hermaphroditic (monoecious), possessing both testes and ovaries, though they still typically cross-fertilise with another individual.

questions.question: The striking transformation of a tadpole into an adult frog, involving major changes in body form, is an example of:
questions.explanation: Metamorphosis is a marked, often abrupt change in body form during development, as seen when a gill-breathing, tailed tadpole transforms into a lung-breathing adult frog.

questions.question: The tendency of an organism to maintain a relatively stable internal environment despite external changes is called:
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the physiological process by which internal conditions (e.g. temperature, pH, water balance) are kept relatively constant regardless of external fluctuations.

questions.question: According to Charles Darwin's theory, individuals with heritable traits best suited to their environment tend to survive and reproduce more successfully. This process is called:
questions.explanation: Natural selection, proposed by Darwin, is the differential survival and reproduction of individuals due to heritable variation in traits suited to the environment.

questions.question: A structural, physiological, or behavioural trait that improves an organism's chances of survival and reproduction in its environment is called a(n):
questions.explanation: An adaptation is any inherited trait shaped by natural selection that enhances an organism's fitness in its particular environment.

questions.question: In ecology, the specific place where an organism normally lives is called its:
questions.explanation: A habitat is the physical location or environment where an organism lives, whereas its niche describes its functional role within that habitat.

questions.question: A group of individuals of the same species living and interbreeding in a given area at a given time is called a:
questions.explanation: A population consists of all the members of one species occupying a defined area and capable of interbreeding, distinct from a community which includes multiple species.

questions.question: All the different populations of species living and interacting together in a given area make up a(n):
questions.explanation: A biological community comprises all the interacting populations of different species that coexist in a given area at a given time.

questions.question: A biological community together with the non-living (abiotic) components of its environment, interacting as a functional unit, is called a(n):
questions.explanation: An ecosystem is the combination of a biotic community and its abiotic environment, linked by flows of energy and cycling of nutrients.

questions.question: The optical instrument most commonly used in an introductory zoology laboratory to view small specimens such as protozoa and blood cells is the:
questions.explanation: The compound light microscope, using two or more lenses, is the standard instrument for viewing microscopic specimens in undergraduate zoology laboratories.

questions.question: Formalin (formaldehyde solution) is commonly used in the zoology laboratory to:
questions.explanation: Formalin is a widely used fixative and preservative that prevents decay and maintains the structural integrity of animal specimens for study.

questions.question: Which pair of phyla is correctly matched with a diagnostic feature?
questions.explanation: Nematocysts, housed in cnidocytes, are the unique stinging organelles that define the Cnidaria; the other pairings mismatch phylum and feature.

questions.question: A student observing an unfamiliar aquatic animal notes: unsegmented body, single muscular foot, visceral mass covered by a mantle that secretes a calcareous shell. The animal most likely belongs to phylum:
questions.explanation: A muscular foot, visceral mass, mantle, and shell are the classic diagnostic combination of features used to identify molluscs.
